intro: The SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam was conducted on 6 October 2026 across three shifts. Shift 1 and Shift 2 have reported summaries, while Shift 3 is pending and its analysis will be added after the shift. The difficulty levels and good‑attempt percentages shown are unofficial and based on candidate feedback; the SSC normally normalises scores across shifts to ensure comparability. Travel and technical issues were noted for some candidates in Shift 1.

shifts.summary: Candidates reported mixed difficulty across sections. Reasoning was described as both high and easy, while GA ranged from easy to moderate. Quantitative items were seen as easy by some and difficult by others, and English difficulty varied from easy to moderate. Travel and technical issues affected some test‑takers.

sections.name: General Intelligence & Reasoning
sections.notes: Reports differ on reasoning difficulty, some calling it high, others easy or moderate. Topics included geometry, number series, coding‑decoding, analogy, matrix, similarity and slog questions.

sections.name: General Awareness
sections.notes: GA questions covered committees, national games, constitutional articles and recent current affairs. Difficulty assessments ranged from easy to moderate.

sections.name: Quantitative Aptitude
sections.notes: Quantitative difficulty was reported from easy to difficult, with many lengthy calculations. Topics spanned trigonometry, compound interest, mensuration, advanced arithmetic and geometry.

sections.name: English Comprehension
sections.notes: English difficulty ranged from easy reading comprehension to moderate spelling and grammar questions. Topics included comprehension, spelling, active/passive transformation, idioms, vocabulary and grammar spotting.

observations: Centre locations far from candidates caused travel cost and time problems.
Sectional timer caused time shortage and missed questions, especially in Math.
Mouse lag and click registration issues were reported during the exam.
Candidates praised coaching (e.g., Rakesh Yadav's classes) as helpful.
disagreements: Overall difficulty reported as Moderate, Difficult, Easy and Easy to Moderate across sources.
Overall good attempts varied from 70‑76 to 92, with no consensus.
Reasoning difficulty described as High, Easy, Moderate and Easy in different reports.
Quant difficulty ranged from Easy to Difficult, and English difficulty from Easy to Difficult.

Good‑attempt percentages were provided but differ between sources. No specific topics or question counts were mentioned. No asked questions were listed.

faqs.q: What was the overall difficulty reported for the SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam on 6 October 2026?
faqs.a: Shift 1 did not provide an overall difficulty rating, Shift 2 was reported as easy across all sections, and Shift 3 has not yet been held, so its overall difficulty will be added after the shift.

faqs.q: How did candidates describe the difficulty of individual sections on 6 October 2026?
faqs.a: For Shift 1, candidates said reasoning ranged from high to easy, general ability from easy to moderate, quantitative items were seen as both easy and difficult, and English varied from easy to moderate. Shift 2 was uniformly described as easy for reasoning, general ability, quantitative, and English. No section data is available for Shift 3 yet.

faqs.q: Are the good‑attempt percentages for the 6 October 2026 SSC CGL Tier 1 exam reliable?
faqs.a: Good‑attempt percentages were not reported for Shift 1 and are only partially available for Shift 2, with differing figures from various sources. Because these numbers are unofficial and derived from candidate feedback, they should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.

faqs.q: When will the analysis for Shift 3 of the 6 October 2026 SSC CGL Tier 1 exam be available?
faqs.a: Shift 3 has not been held yet; its analysis will be added after the shift is completed.

faqs.q: How does the SSC normalise scores across the shifts for the 6 October 2026 Tier 1 exam?
faqs.a: The SSC applies a normalisation process that adjusts raw scores from each shift to a common scale, ensuring that candidates are compared fairly regardless of the shift they attended. This practice is standard for multi‑shift examinations.
